extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on representing a character's inner life and point of view by dramatizing the surface of thought (scenes, images, gestures) rather than by direct exposition. Covers when to use or dispense with a narrator, how to reveal hidden facts, and how to render undramatic subjects dramatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a character's consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind must be made intelligible by a direct view of its surface: 'The immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next and the next, will then take up the tale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the passing images that cross a character's mind as enactments onstage; do not attempt to penetrate behind the outer aspect. Example: Strether’s mind is 'dramatized' so that nothing is shown but surface images anyone might detect. Keep representation to observable mental gestures, impressions, and images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell; avoid summary or report
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere account of a mind's working after the fact 'is lacking in force, it is statement where we look for demonstration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not replace scenes with tabulations of reasons or retrospective summaries. To show change of attitude, give successive moments and scenes rather than narrated explanations; let the reader witness the process rather than be told it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial intrusion; accept nothing on authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Henry James 'knows all there is to know of Strether, but he most carefully refrains from using his knowledge. He wishes us to accept nothing from him, on authority—only to watch and learn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from using omniscient authorial asides or supplying the reader with facts about characters that are not visible in the scene. Trust the dramatization to communicate what the reader needs to infer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrained revelation produces suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: If a narrator (or the author) begins to expound the substance of a character's mind, 'he must at once give us the whole of it... and so, too, if the book were cast autobiographically and Strether spoke in person; he could not hold back.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial disclosure by a character-narrator is misleading; restraint and piecemeal revelation (showing rather than telling) create suspense and preserve dramatic effect. Anti-pattern: a first-person narrator who retrospectively explains inner motives in full, thereby deflating immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a single, consistent point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Ambassadors is a story which is seen from one man’s point of view... the one-sided vision is strictly enjoined by the method of the whole book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the center of vision within the chosen character so that description and scenes are filtered through that consciousness. Even when scenes appear more objective, they should remain anchored in that point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes and dialogue to supply necessary backstory
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversation 'puts the reader in possession of all the past facts of the situation which it is necessary for him to know; a scene thus takes the place of that “harking back to make up.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatized scenes that reveal past facts organically (through talk and action) over lumps of narrative exposition. Let dialogue enact what would otherwise be recounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat undramatic subjects dramatically by animating description
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic rule 'animates the actual elements of the picture, and makes a drama of these' so that even undramatic, pictorial subjects gain relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a subject seems 'entirely undramatic' (a condition, situation, or inward state), animate its descriptive elements—gestures, looks, pauses—so the subject enacts itself and attains dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid peppering scenes with irrelevant dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is not managed by peppering the surface with animated dialogue... the end of this is only to cheapen and discredit their talk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every piece of dialogue contributes to the subject or the dramatization. Avoid inserting talk merely to enliven prose; irrelevant chatter undermines the impact of genuinely important speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let implication and small cues reveal hidden facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'strange look or a pause or a sudden hasty motion' may betray everything; the 'enlightening word' that finally gives the reader a fact may pass unnoticed at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gestures, glances, pauses, and small verbal cues to suggest deeper facts rather than stating them. Structure the text so that a reader may later identify the moment where the hidden fact was implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple peripheral glimpses (stereoscopic method) to build depth
rubrics_metrics.description: By seeing 'to left and right, as far as possible, just as with two eyes, stereoscopically, we shape... the image will be so raised out of its setting' and gain solidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surround a central fact with many peripheral views—different moments, settings, interactions—so that the reader apprehends the subject's weight and form from several angles rather than from a single flat account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve the narrator unless the narrator adds value (economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself... he is better dispensed with and put out of the way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use an explicit narrator when their perspective or economy (e.g., panoramic chronicle, necessary commentary) contributes materially. If the narrator does not enhance the effect, assign the point of view to the scene and the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let a character-narrator begin partial exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If he once begins [to tell all], he must at once give us the whole of it, must let us into every secret without delay, or his exposition is plainly misleading.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having a character-narrator intermittently slip into explanatory exposition. Either the narrator fully owns the explanatory role (and accepts consequences) or the method should remain dramatized and deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dramatization to give inner life solidity and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatization gives 'Solidity, weight, a third dimension' to a character's case that mere emphasis or plain words cannot produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make emotional or moral conditions feel substantial, stage their peripheral, surface manifestations consistently. The enactment of small moments yields a sense of real, dimensional experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show incremental inner change through multiplied moments
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a character 'is slowly turning upon himself and looking in another direction' the author should 'bring his mind into view at the different moments... to multiply these glimpses until the silent change is apparent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray psychological transformation by repeating and varying small moments and impressions over time rather than by single proclamations of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer methods and experiment with mixtures of technique
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'an immense variety of possible modulations, mixtures, harmonies of method, yet untried, are open to it'—the novelist can lay method upon method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to combining approaches (dramatic enactment, selective narration, scene-based exposition) to achieve nuanced effects. Formal experimentation with method is encouraged to expand the novel's resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay on the observable surface; drama asks the spectator to judge by appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Below the surface, behind the outer aspect of his mind, we do not penetrate; this is drama, and in drama the spectator must judge by appearances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the dramatic presentation limited to what can be perceived—expressions, gestures, speech, and immediate thoughts. Do not intrude into inaccessible 'hidden depths' except when a methodological reason justifies it.
